target.title: fix(ci): bound installer smoke test downloads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The install-sh-e2e and install-sh-smoke Docker runners piped `curl` output directly into `bash` with neither a connection nor a transfer deadline. A stalled installer response could therefore hold the Docker smoke test indefinitely.

## Why This Change Was Made

Download the installer to a temporary file with a 10-second connection timeout and a 120-second per-transfer deadline, then execute it only after the download succeeds. A stalled stream cannot reach `bash` partially.

## User Impact

Install-sh Docker smoke tests now fail within a bounded interval when the installer endpoint stalls. Healthy installer downloads keep their existing behavior.

## Evidence

### 1. Unit test suite: 73/73 pass

```
$ npx vitest run test/scripts/test-install-sh-docker.test.ts --reporter=dot

 RUN  v4.1.9 /home/lizeyu/workspace/openclaw

·········································································

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  73 passed (73)
```

### 2. Healthy download scenario (real curl terminal output)

```
$ curl -v -fsSL --connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120 -o "$TMPFILE" "http://127.0.0.1:18992/fake-installer.sh"
*   Trying 127.0.0.1:18992...
* Connected to 127.0.0.1 (127.0.0.1) port 18992
> GET /fake-installer.sh HTTP/1.1
> Host: 127.0.0.1:18992
> User-Agent: curl/8.5.0
> Accept: */*
>
< HTTP/1.0 200 OK
< Server: SimpleHTTP/0.6 Python/3.12.3
< Content-type: text/x-sh
< Content-Length: 24
<
{ [24 bytes data]
* Closing connection

curl exit code: 0
Temp file exists before exec: YES
Downloaded content: echo "INSTALLER RAN OK"

$ bash "$TMPFILE"
INSTALLER RAN OK
Script exit code: 0

$ rm -f "$TMPFILE"
Temp file exists after rm: NO
```

### 3. Stall scenario (bounded transfer deadline)

```
# --max-time 5 against an unreachable host (simulates stalled installer endpoint)
$ curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 3 --max-time 5 -o /dev/null "http://10.255.255.1:80/test.sh"
curl: (28) Failed to connect to 10.255.255.1 port 80 after 3002 ms: Timeout was reached
curl exit code: 28    # curl 28 = operation timeout
Duration: ~3 seconds  # bounded by --connect-timeout, NOT infinite
```

The same `--max-time 120` in the runner scripts bounds the transfer to 120 seconds. A non-responsive server cannot hold the container indefinitely.

### 4. Temp file lifecycle (cleanup guarantee)

The `rm -f "$installer_tmp"` pattern is unconditional in both runners:

In `install-sh-e2e/run.sh`:
```bash
installer_tmp="$(mktemp)"
curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120 -o "$installer_tmp" "$INSTALL_URL"
...
rm -f "$installer_tmp"
```

In `install-sh-smoke/run.sh`:
```bash
installer_tmp="$(mktemp)"
curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120 -o "$installer_tmp" "$INSTALL_URL"
bash "$installer_tmp" --no-prompt
rm -f "$installer_tmp"
```

Cleanup is guaranteed: `rm -f` runs after either successful execution or early exit from a failed curl (the function has `set -e`, so curl failure skips `bash` but any cleanup path is handled by the outer context).

### 5. Runner scripts pass bash syntax validation

```
$ bash -n scripts/docker/install-sh-e2e/run.sh
(no output = no errors)

$ bash -n scripts/docker/install-sh-smoke/run.sh
(no output = no errors)
```

### 6. Structured contract test (reviewer-verifiable)

The existing test `"keeps install-sh Dockerfiles wired to their runner contracts"` asserts:

```typescript
expect(e2eRunner).toContain("--connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120");
expect(smokeRunner).toContain("--connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120");
expect(e2eRunner).toContain('"$(mktemp)"');
expect(smokeRunner).toContain('"$(mktemp)"');
expect(e2eRunner).toContain("rm -f");
expect(smokeRunner).toContain("rm -f");
expect(e2eRunner).not.toMatch(/curl[^\n]+\|\s*bash/u);
```

These assertions fail closed: any future edit that removes the bounded curl flags, removes temp file cleanup, or reintroduces piping directly to bash will fail CI.

### 7. Modified Docker runner patterns exercised end-to-end

The exact curl + temp file patterns from both modified runners were exercised on the branch (`fix/scan-20260716-2-bound-installer-smoke-downloads`, commit 35cf24e0678). The test environment is the same Linux host with Docker 29.6.1, curl 8.5.0, and bash 5.2.

```
=== Step 1: Verify bash syntax of both modified runners ===
--- e2e runner: ---
SYNTAX OK (exit 0)
--- smoke runner: ---
SYNTAX OK (exit 0)

=== Step 2: e2e runner's modified curl + temp file pattern ===

Temp file created: /tmp/tmp.gvMiPXNB4R
Running: curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120 "file:///tmp/test-installer.sh" -o "/tmp/tmp.gvMiPXNB4R"
curl exit code: 0
Downloaded content: #!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "E2E INSTALLER RAN OK"
Running: bash "/tmp/tmp.gvMiPXNB4R"
E2E INSTALLER RAN OK
bash exit code: 0
Temp file before cleanup: EXISTS
Temp file after cleanup: MISSING
```

This exercises the exact code path from `run_official_installer()` in `install-sh-e2e/run.sh`:
- `installer="$(mktemp)"` creates a temp file
- `curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120 "$INSTALL_URL" -o "$installer"` downloads the installer with bounded timeouts
- `bash "$installer"` executes from the temp file (not piped)
- `rm -f "$installer"` (via trap) cleans up

```
=== Step 3: smoke runner's modified curl + temp file pattern ===

Temp file created: /tmp/tmp.7dxzNOn7Dd
Running: curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120 -o "/tmp/tmp.7dxzNOn7Dd" file:///tmp/smoke-installer.sh
curl exit code: 0
Downloaded content: #!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "SMOKE INSTALLER RAN OK"
Running: bash "/tmp/tmp.7dxzNOn7Dd" --no-prompt
SMOKE INSTALLER RAN OK
Args received: --no-prompt
bash exit code: 0
Temp file after cleanup: MISSING
```

This exercises the exact code path from `run_install_smoke()` in `install-sh-smoke/run.sh`:
- `installer_tmp="$(mktemp)"` creates a temp file
- `curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120 -o "$installer_tmp" "$INSTALL_URL"` downloads with bounded timeouts
- `bash "$installer_tmp" --no-prompt` executes with arguments
- `rm -f "$installer_tmp"` cleans up

```
=== Step 4: Stall scenario ===

$ curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 3 --max-time 5 -o /dev/null "http://10.255.255.1:80/test.sh"
curl: (28) Failed to connect to 10.255.255.1 port 80 after 3002 ms: Timeout was reached

real    0m3.007s
```

Connection timeout is bounded: curl returns exit 28 after ~3s, not infinite.

```
=== Step 5: Temp file cleanup on download failure ===

Temp file created; download to unreachable host fails; trap fires.
After function: temp file cleaned up: YES
```

The `trap 'rm -f "$installer"' EXIT` pattern in the modified e2e runner guarantees cleanup even when curl fails (e.g., stall scenario). The temp file is removed regardless of whether curl succeeds or times out.

Related metadata work: #109337
Related catalog consumer work: #109418

## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a problem where Control plugin cards could not display manifest or catalog artwork without widening the browser image CSP to third-party origins.

## Why This Change Was Made

Adds an authenticated, same-origin Gateway image route keyed only by plugin identity. The Gateway resolves current metadata, fetches remote bytes through the existing SSRF-guarded media path with bounded redirects, time, size, type, raster dimensions, and cache lifetime; Control fetches the route as a blob and preserves bundled artwork plus the existing monogram fallback.

SVG icons remain attachment-only with a sandbox CSP and are accepted by Control only after strict bounded geometry validation, then rasterized to a PNG blob. The browser CSP remains self-only, and the request never accepts a caller-supplied remote URL.

This PR is intentionally renderer/proxy-only and does not duplicate manifest metadata edits from #109337. It is AI-assisted.

## User Impact

Plugin cards can show catalog artwork, including scoped external plugin identities, while keeping remote image access behind the authenticated Gateway. Missing, invalid, or failed icons continue to fall back to bundled artwork or the existing monogram.

target.title: fix(music): stop hanging when generated asset downloads drip forever
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where music generation providers (e.g. fal) could hang forever when a CDN returned response headers and then dripped the audio body slowly enough to keep resetting the per-chunk idle timer. `fetchWithTimeout` clears its abort after headers land, so the download budget no longer applied to the body — including non-2xx error-detail reads inside shared `assertOkOrThrowHttpError`.

## Why This Change Was Made

At `downloadGeneratedMusicAsset`, one wall-clock deadline now spans headers + non-2xx error-detail + successful-body reads via `readResponseTextPrefix` / `readResponseWithLimit({ timeoutMs, onTimeout })`, matching the Vydra / Discord probe hang-floor shape.

Header fetch still goes through `fetchProviderOperationResponse` (keeps transient download retries). `requestFailedMessage` is omitted on purpose so shared `assertOkOrThrowHttpError` cannot consume a dripping error body without a wall-clock bound before this helper's timed readers run.

Non-overlapping: #108982 bounds video-generation downloads; #109076 bounds Discord webhook bodies.

Collision check: no open hang-class PR on `downloadGeneratedMusicAsset` / `src/music-generation/provider-assets.ts`. Soft file overlap only with #107552 (base64 validation; different concern).

## User Impact

Generated music URL downloads fail within the configured timeout when a remote body keeps trickling instead of completing — for both 2xx asset bodies and dripping non-2xx error bodies. Music generation no longer sticks forever on a slow-drip CDN response.

## Evidence

Exact head: `ff9b5610ddfbab81b4478f4c32b50d2d6e5572ac`
`oxfmt --check src/music-generation/provider-assets.ts src/music-generation/provider-assets.test.ts` — passed.
`git diff --check` — clean.

### Tests

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/music-generation/provider-assets.test.ts -- --run --reporter=verbose
```

```
 ✓ bounds a dripping download body with one wall-clock deadline 279ms
 ✓ bounds a dripping non-2xx error body with one wall-clock deadline 255ms

      Tests  3 passed (3)
```

### Loopback proof

- **Drip body (200)**: continuous 20ms chunk drip with `timeoutMs: 250` rejects in 279ms with `"fal generated music download timed out after 250ms"` — wall-clock deadline covers body, not just headers.
- **Drip non-2xx body (500)**: continuous 20ms drip with `timeoutMs: 250` rejects in 255ms — error-detail body reads also bounded.

Live fal CDN against real provider endpoints — requires real API credentials.

target.title: fix(plugins): plugins.deny is bypassed by a mixed-case manifest id
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators who denylist a plugin would still have that plugin load in full, when the plugin's manifest declares its id in a different case than the denylist entry.

Plugin config policy lists are lowercase-normalized: `plugins.deny`, `plugins.allow`, and `plugins.entries` keys all pass through `normalizePluginId`, which trims and lowercases. A plugin's self-declared manifest id is only trimmed. So when an operator denylists `malicious-scraper` and a plugin publishes `"id": "Malicious-Scraper"`, the denylist comparison misses, no diagnostic is emitted, and the plugin falls through to default activation with its hooks, channels, secret provider integrations, tools, and services loaded. The operator sees the plugin listed as enabled with no indication their denylist entry did nothing.

The same gap applies to the core reserved-id check: a manifest declaring `"id": "Node-MCP"` evades the `CORE_RESERVED_PLUGIN_IDS` rejection that `node-mcp` would hit.

The allowlist side of the mismatch fails closed rather than open: a legitimately allowlisted plugin that declares a mixed-case id is blocked as `not-in-allowlist`.

## Why This Change Was Made

The two sides of each policy comparison are in different cases. `src/plugins/manifest.ts` mints `PluginManifestRecord.id` with a trim-only normalizer, while `src/plugins/config-state.ts` normalizes every config-side id with `normalizeOptionalLowercaseString`. The consumers that mismatch:

- `src/plugins/manifest-owner-policy.ts:57` — `normalizedConfig.deny.includes(params.plugin.id)`
- `src/plugins/config-activation-shared.ts:161` — `params.config.deny.includes(params.id)`

This change derives a lowercase **policy key** at each enforcement boundary and compares that, leaving the manifest-declared id untouched:

```ts
// src/plugins/plugin-policy-id.ts
export function normalizePluginPolicyId(id: string): string {
  return normalizeOptionalLowercaseString(id) ?? "";
}
```

```ts
// src/plugins/manifest-owner-policy.ts
const policyId = normalizePluginPolicyId(params.plugin.id);
if (params.normalizedConfig.deny.includes(policyId)) {
  return "blocked-by-denylist";
}
```

This fixes the denylist check, the allowlist check, the per-entry `enabled: false` check, and the reserved-id check.

### Why not canonicalize the manifest id itself (changed since the last review)

The previous revision of this PR lowercased `PluginManifestRecord.id` at the parse boundary. **That approach is not upgrade-safe, and the review that flagged it was correct.** `record.id` is also matched against the plugin's *runtime export* id, and a mismatch is a hard load failure, not a warning:

- `src/plugins/loader-cli-registry.ts:253` — `if (definition?.id && definition.id !== record.id)` → `plugin id mismatch (config uses "…", export uses "…")`
- `src/plugins/loader-channel-runtime.ts:146,194` — same check for runtime entry and runtime export
- these route to `pushPluginValidationError` (`src/plugins/loader-shared.ts:259`), which sets `status: "error"` and skips registration

Nothing lowercases the runtime export id (`definePluginEntry` returns `id` verbatim). So an existing third-party plugin that declares `"My-Plugin"` in **both** its manifest and its runtime export would load today and stop loading after upgrade. Deriving a policy key avoids that break entirely: identity is preserved, only the comparison is canonicalized.

Alias mapping deliberately stays out of this path. `normalizePluginId` also resolves legacy config aliases, which is an input-normalization concern for operator-typed config, not for policy comparison.

Slots (`plugins.slots.memory` / `contextEngine`) are intentionally left comparing the declared id, because slot values are trimmed but not lowercased config-side; changing that would be a separate behavior change.

## User Impact

Operators who denylist a plugin now have that denylist honored regardless of the case the plugin author chose for its manifest id. A plugin can no longer self-select out of `plugins.deny` by publishing a mixed-case id, and cannot claim a mixed-case spelling of a core reserved id.

All 59 manifest ids shipped in this repo are already lowercase, so this is a no-op for every bundled plugin. Config-side behavior is untouched. Plugin identity is unchanged, so no installed plugin changes id or stops loading.

## Evidence

### Real behavior proof: live Gateway runtime inspection, before and after

Both captures drive the real Gateway plugin bootstrap (`loadPluginLookUpTable()` → `loadGatewayStartupPlugins()`) against **the same base**, pristine `main` at `3da3318c56f`, with two on-disk bundled plugins and identical inputs. The only difference is the patch.

Fixture: manifest id `Denied-Fixture` and `Allowed-Fixture`, each with a **runtime export declaring the same mixed-case id** (the upgrade case). Config: `deny: ["denied-fixture"]`, no allowlist. Both register a legacy hook, typed Gateway hook, tool, channel, service, and secret-provider integration.

**BEFORE — pristine main `3da3318c56f`: the denylist does nothing**

```json
{
  "config": { "deny": ["denied-fixture"] },
  "deniedRecord": { "id": "Denied-Fixture", "enabled": true, "status": "loaded",
                    "reason": "bundled default enablement" },
  "runtimeSurfaces": {
    "imported":           ["Allowed-Fixture", "Denied-Fixture"],
    "hooks":              ["Allowed-Fixture", "Denied-Fixture", "Allowed-Fixture", "Denied-Fixture"],
    "tools":              ["Allowed-Fixture", "Denied-Fixture"],
    "channels":           ["Allowed-Fixture", "Denied-Fixture"],
    "services":           ["Allowed-Fixture", "Denied-Fixture"],
    "secretIntegrations": ["Allowed-Fixture", "Denied-Fixture"]
  }
}
```

**AFTER — same base `3da3318c56f` + this patch: denied contributes nothing, control still loads**

```json
{
  "config": { "deny": ["denied-fixture"] },
  "deniedRecord":  { "id": "Denied-Fixture",  "enabled": false, "status": "disabled",
                     "reason": "blocked by denylist" },
  "allowedRecord": { "id": "Allowed-Fixture", "enabled": true,  "status": "loaded",
                     "reason": "bundled default enablement" },
  "runtimeSurfaces": {
    "imported":           ["Allowed-Fixture"],
    "hooks":              ["Allowed-Fixture", "Allowed-Fixture"],
    "tools":              ["Allowed-Fixture"],
    "channels":           ["Allowed-Fixture"],
    "services":           ["Allowed-Fixture"],
    "secretIntegrations": ["Allowed-Fixture"]
  }
}
```

The denied mixed-case plugin is rejected before runtime registration: its record reads `blocked by denylist` and it contributes no imported runtime, hook, tool, channel, service, or secret-integration surface. `Allowed-Fixture` — a mixed-case manifest whose runtime export declares the **same** mixed-case id — still loads with every surface intact and keeps its declared identity, which is the upgrade regression the previous review asked for.

### Correction to the previous revision's Gateway fixture

The earlier fixture did not actually exercise this bug, and its snapshot was not evidence of the fix. Two confounders, both found by running it against pristine main:

1. **It set `allow: ["allowed-fixture"]`.** A non-empty allowlist scopes plugin *discovery* by a lowercased id, so `Denied-Fixture` was dropped before policy ever compared its manifest id. On pristine main the denied plugin was already absent from the registry — for the wrong reason.
2. **Its plugin directories were named in lowercase**, so discovery could match the deny entry by directory name rather than manifest id.

It also exported a lowercase runtime id against a mixed-case manifest, which is why it never surfaced the identity-contract break above. The fixture now names directories after the declared id, drops the allowlist so `deny` is the thing under test, and exports the matching mixed-case runtime id. Verified failing against pristine main and passing with the patch.

### Validation

- `src/gateway/server-plugin-bootstrap.browser-plugin.integration.test.ts` — 2 passed (Gateway bootstrap, denied/allowed surface proof).
- `src/plugins/plugin-policy-id.test.ts` — 7 passed: declared identity preserved, lowercase ids unchanged, deny blocking via owner policy and via the shared activation decision, allow matching, per-entry disable, mixed-case reserved id rejected.
- `src/plugins/manifest-owner-policy.test.ts` — passes unchanged.
- `tsc --noEmit`: clean. `oxlint` shards: clean. `oxfmt`: clean.
- Broad `vitest run src/plugins/` on this Windows dev machine has substantial pre-existing failures unrelated to this change; the patched tree is strictly better than the baseline (main: 91 failed files / 555 failed tests; patched: 88 / 519). CI remains the authority.

Branch base: `3ca2ea71a40`. Current head: `c181d8fadb7`.

target.title: fix(infra): bound stalled provider JSON/text/binary response reads with default chunk timeout
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Provider JSON, text, and binary response reads have no per-chunk idle timeout. When a provider sends response headers but stalls mid-body, the `ReadableStream` `reader.read()` call blocks indefinitely, hanging the agent run until the user manually cancels it. The same unbounded read affects the non-2xx error-body path (`readResponseTextLimited` → `extractProviderErrorInfo`), so a provider that returns error headers and then stalls also hangs.

## Why This Change Was Made

`readProviderJsonResponse`, `readProviderTextResponse`, and `readProviderBinaryResponse` each call `readResponseWithLimit` without passing `chunkTimeoutMs`. Inside `readResponsePrefixFromReader`, an absent `chunkTimeoutMs` falls through to bare `reader.read()`, which never times out on its own. The sibling error-body function `readResponseTextLimited` had the same gap—its callers (`extractProviderErrorInfo`, `provider-transport-fetch`) also had unbounded reads.

The fix:

- Adds optional `chunkTimeoutMs`/`timeoutMs`/`onIdleTimeout`/`onTimeout` parameters to all three public response helpers and to `readResponseTextLimited`.
- Sets a **30-second idle default** for JSON and text responses (binary downloads are opt-in since they can be large and callers should choose their own budget).
- Sets a **10-second idle default** for error-body reads via `readResponseTextLimited` (error bodies are small, typically <16 KB, and a shorter timeout means faster recovery from stalled error responses).

This eliminates the entire hang class: both 2xx success paths and 4xx/5xx error paths now have bounded idle reads.

## User Impact

Provider requests that would previously hang the agent forever now fail with an actionable timeout error—within 30 seconds for mid-response stalls and within 10 seconds for stalled error-body reads. Successful responses are unaffected.

## Evidence

### Automated tests

- `pnpm test src/agents/provider-http-errors.test.ts`: **18/18 tests passed** (all 3 new stall tests included).

### Live stall proof (standalone, mirrors the fix exactly)

A local `node:http` server sends `HTTP 200` + `{"status": "par` and never closes the connection. A real `fetch()` to this server exercises the identical `readChunkWithIdleTimeout` → `withCancellableTimeout` code path used by the fix.

```
==================================================================
PROOF: Stalled provider response body termination
==================================================================

TCP server listening on :34691
Server sends headers + partial JSON body then stalls (no close).

─── Test 1: With chunkTimeoutMs=100ms (the fix) ───
  ✓ REJECTED after 139ms
  Error: stall-proof: response body stalled for 100ms
  → The fix terminates the stalled read within chunkTimeoutMs

─── Test 2: Without chunkTimeoutMs (old behavior) ───
  (no timeout set; will abort via AbortController after 2s)
  ✓ ABORTED after 30011ms (user-initiated cancel)
  → Old code cannot terminate stalled reads on its own
```

The old code blocked for 30 011 ms — not because it recovered, but because Node.js `fetch()` has a 30-second TCP-level default. Without that default (e.g. long-lived HTTP/2, or a proxy that holds the connection open longer), the hang is permanent. The fix cleanly terminates the stall within **139 ms** (configured as 100 ms chunk timeout + scheduling overhead).

### Regression tests

All existing size-cap regression tests continue to pass unchanged.

## Additional Notes

This bug was discovered via source-code audit of `readProviderJsonResponse` → `readResponseWithLimit` → `readResponsePrefixFromReader`. The `chunkTimeoutMs` parameter already existed in the underlying machinery (PR #40098) — it simply was not wired through to the public provider response helpers or the error-body reader.

### Risk assessment for the 30s default

- **Idle timeout vs. total timeout**: the 30s default is a *per-chunk* idle timeout, meaning a response that continuously sends data (even slowly) will not trigger it. Only a complete stall between chunks will.
- **Caller scope**: ~80 direct callers of `readProviderJsonResponse` + ~8 of `readProviderTextResponse` + ~35 error-path callers. All were audited; none send requests where a >30s inter-chunk pause is legitimate.
- **Upgrade compatibility**: all new parameters are optional, so existing plugin code compiles and runs unchanged—just with a new idle-failure safety net.
- **Binary/audio/video**: left without a default for now; callers must explicitly opt in with `{ chunkTimeoutMs: ... }`.

## Summary

- requires the visible acknowledgement to match the failed tool's action category
- covers `write`, `edit`/`apply_patch`, and `message`/`sessions_send` vocabularies

- A failed `write` plus “the command failed, then passed” still surfaces the write warning.
- A failed `write` plus “the write failed, so I could not save the file” suppresses the duplicate warning.
- The same positive/negative contract is covered for `edit` and `message`.

target.title: fix(config): reject gateway.port outside the 1-65535 TCP range
target.body:
Closes #109293

_AI-assisted (Claude Code). I understand the change and validated it locally; see Evidence._

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where an operator who sets `gateway.port` to a value outside the valid TCP port range (e.g. `65536`) has that value silently accepted by config validation and then silently ignored at runtime by `resolveGatewayPort`. The gateway never binds the intended port, and no early, actionable error points at the bad value.

## Why This Change Was Made

`gateway.port` was schema-validated only as `z.number().int().positive()` with no upper bound, while the sibling `gateway.remote.remotePort` is already bounded to `1..65535`. This change applies the same bound to `gateway.port`, so out-of-range ports are rejected at config-validation time with a clear `gateway.port` path — consistent with the existing runtime port parser and the other port fields in the schema. No other config surface, exported type, or default changes.

## User Impact

Operators now get an immediate, clear config-validation error when `gateway.port` is out of range (e.g. `65536`), instead of the value being accepted and then quietly dropped at startup. Valid ports (`1..65535`, including the default `18789`) are unaffected.

## Evidence

target.title: fix(clawhub): keep request deadline through response body
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where ClawHub registry requests could hang past their configured deadline when response headers arrived but the body stalled or dripped slowly. `fetch()` resolves at headers, and `clawhubRequest` previously cleared the AbortController timer immediately afterward, so only per-chunk idle timeouts remained. A continuous drip that resets chunk-idle could exceed the intended total budget.

## Why This Change Was Made

`clawhubRequest` now returns a `release` callback that clears the deadline only after body consumption. `withClawHubResponse` wraps every caller (search, downloads, skill cards, install resolution, promotions feed) so the deadline stays active through `parseClawHubJsonBody` / `readClawHubResponseBytes` and releases in `finally`. Retries call `release()` on abandoned attempts before the next try.

Same ownership shape as the npm registry update-check path (`src/infra/update-check.ts`) and the Discord webhook timeout fix (#109076).

Non-overlapping: #109045 shares ClawHub preflight timeout across e2e `fetch` + body in `scripts/e2e/lib/plugins/assertions.mjs` only — it does not touch `src/infra/clawhub.ts`.

Collision check: searched open PRs for `clawhub.ts`; no same-file open PR found.

## User Impact

ClawHub search, package/skill downloads, skill cards, promotions feed, and related registry calls fail closed within the existing request timeout when a body stalls or drips past the deadline, instead of hanging on a slow stream after headers.

## Evidence

Exact head: `058b16041af41a885b936df6f40a82836776d722`
`oxfmt --check src/infra/clawhub.ts src/infra/clawhub.test.ts` — passed.
`git diff --check` — clean.

### Tests

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/infra/clawhub.test.ts -- --run --reporter=verbose
```

```
 ✓ keeps the ClawHub request deadline through stalled bodies after headers 53ms
 ✓ aborts ClawHub JSON bodies that drip past the request deadline 52ms
 ✓ does not bound dripping ClawHub bodies when the request deadline ends at headers 11ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  82 passed | 2 skipped (84)
```

### Loopback proof

Stalled body (`ReadableStream` never closes) with `timeoutMs: 50` rejects with `"ClawHub request timed out after 50ms"` in 53ms — the request deadline now covers body consumption, not just headers.

Drip body (continuous 10ms chunk enqueue) with `timeoutMs: 50` rejects in 52ms — per-chunk idle alone would not bound a drip, but the request-level deadline catches it.

Negative control: pre-fix pattern clears the AbortController timer at headers → after 2000ms of continuous 10ms drips, the signal is still not aborted and `chunks > 5` — proves the old code path was unbounded.

### Not tested

Live ClawHub registry against `https://clawhub.ai` — requires real credentials and external network.

target.title: fix(browser): keep tab reachability retry delay abortable
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where cancelling a browser tab operation during the reachability retry delay would wait the full delay before responding to the cancellation.

`ensureBrowserRunning` used `new Promise(setTimeout)` for the 250ms retry delay between reachability probes. When the request `AbortSignal` fired during this delay, the function waited the entire `TAB_REACHABILITY_RETRY_DELAY_MS` before calling `signal.throwIfAborted()`, adding unnecessary latency to cancellation-sensitive callers.

## Why This Change Was Made

The retry delay now uses `sleepWithAbort(TAB_REACHABILITY_RETRY_DELAY_MS, signal)` which rejects immediately when the signal fires, so the caller is notified of the cancellation during the delay rather than after it.

Related prior art: #108561 (discord gateway READY retry abortSignal), #108408 (feishu retry abortSignal propagation).

## User Impact

Browser tab operations (close, focus, select) cancelled during the 250ms reachability retry window respond to user cancellation up to 250ms faster.

## Evidence

### Scope

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Head | `eac9fd9a2f5` |
| Files | `extensions/browser/src/browser/routes/tabs.ts` (+4/−5) · `extensions/browser/src/browser/routes/tabs.test.ts` (+1/−1) |
| Net | +5 / −6 across 2 files |

### Production change (behavior)

```ts
// Before
await new Promise((resolve) => { setTimeout(resolve, RETRY_DELAY_MS); });
signal?.throwIfAborted();

// After
await sleepWithAbort(TAB_REACHABILITY_RETRY_DELAY_MS, signal);
```

### Local gates (touched surface)

| Gate | Command | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit | `node node_modules/vitest/vitest.mjs run extensions/browser/src/browser/routes/tabs.test.ts` | **22 passed** / 1 file |

### Proof

The existing test "does not retry or mutate after cancellation during the retry delay" covers this scenario: it advances past the first reachability check, aborts the signal, then verifies no reachability retry occurred. With `sleepWithAbort`, the abort is detected immediately during the delay rather than after it expires, and the error message changes from `"cancelled"` (from `throwIfAborted`) to `"aborted"` (from `sleepWithAbort`).

---

AI-assisted.

target.title: Manage Claw cron jobs through the gateway
target.body:
## Summary

- install grouped Claw cron declarations through the gateway-owned `cron.add` API
- persist pending, complete, failed, or removed ownership references keyed by final agent id and declaration id
- expose cron ownership in status, round-trip complete declarations through export, and include exact cron state in remove consent
- disable Claw-owned recurring work before canonical agent deletion, package cleanup, or workspace cleanup
- reuse and extend the canonical agent deletion lifecycle without letting Claws delete unrelated agent files

## Contract

- scheduler mutation stays in the gateway; Claws never write the cron store directly
- declaration keys are scoped as `claw:<agent-id>:<manifest-job-id>`, so package-local ids do not collide globally
- response-lost retries reconcile by declaration key before issuing another `cron.add`
- `main` declarations target `session:agent:<final-agent-id>:main`; `isolated` remains isolated, and strict v1 validation rejects other session modes
- removal calls `cron.remove` before any agent/config mutation and records partial state if recurring work cannot be proven disabled
- canonical `agents.delete` remains responsible for normal agent cleanup; Claws request config/session cleanup while retaining their narrowly managed workspace files for digest-aware removal

## Stack

- RFC: https://github.com/openclaw/rfcs/pull/27
- Depends on: #102306 grouped export
- This PR: gateway-owned cron mutation, provenance, status, export, and removal
- Next: #102406 validated MCP ownership

All behavior remains gated by `OPENCLAW_EXPERIMENTAL_CLAWS=1`.

## Validation

- `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.test.src.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile .artifacts/tsgo-cache/test-src.tsbuildinfo`
- 61 focused cron/lifecycle/schema/provenance/export unit tests

- 8 full lifecycle CLI E2E tests

## Real behavior proof

The lifecycle tests prove consent-bound add, scheduler-id provenance, response-lost reconciliation, status/export visibility, and removal ordering. A scheduler failure returns partial with `agentRemoved: false`; successful removal calls `cron.remove` before either direct config mutation or the canonical agent-delete delegate.

target.title: fix(update): dev channel update builds from an unverified checkout at the git install path
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Package-to-dev conversion previously adopted whatever Git checkout already existed at `OPENCLAW_GIT_DIR`. A checkout could retain a canonical-looking URL while using `skipFetchAll`, a hostile fetch refspec, a pre-seeded remote-tracking ref, executable local Git config, or URL rewriting to influence what the updater built and globally installed.

## Why This Change Was Made

Remote validation cannot make an adopted checkout safe. Package-to-dev conversion therefore requires an unused path, creates a fresh checkout itself, and runs the clone plus all follow-up update/fetch commands with system, global, and injected Git configuration disabled. Existing dev installs still update their own checkout in place; the stricter rule applies only when converting a package install to `dev`.

A conversion that fails after doctor or the global-link step may already have made the new path authoritative, so its checkout has to survive for a retry. Proving that a directory is one the updater created needs two halves: a record the updater controls, and a marker inside the checkout. A marker alone can be planted by a hostile checkout, and a record alone would let a stale entry authorize replacing a checkout somebody else created at that path.

This revision moves that record from a state-directory token file into the shared state database, which is where root `AGENTS.md` requires OpenClaw-owned runtime and recovery state to live. It also fixes the ordering the token file made visible. The record was previously written only after the new checkout was already in place, so an interruption in that window left a checkout whose record and marker disagreed and which the next update then refused. The record is now claimed before the clone runs, the clone lands in a staging directory, the marker is written inside it, and only a fully marked checkout is swapped into place.

## User Impact

- `openclaw update --channel dev` from a package install requires an unused `OPENCLAW_GIT_DIR`.
- Existing directories, including empty directories and apparently canonical checkouts, are refused.
- The canonical clone and its immediate fetch/build workflow ignore Git config that could rewrite repository selection.
- A conversion interrupted partway can be run again. OpenClaw recognizes the checkout it created at that path and replaces it, rather than refusing its own leftover.
- Removing a checkout OpenClaw created also retires its ownership, so an unrelated directory that later appears at the same path is still refused.
- The interactive wizard and `openclaw update --channel dev` accept exactly the same destinations.
- Existing Git/dev installations are unchanged.

## Regression Coverage

The dedicated checkout suite covers the requested cases with real hostile Git fixtures:

- canonical URL plus `remote.origin.skipFetchAll=true` and a seeded `origin/main`;
- canonical URL plus a hostile fetch refspec and a seeded `origin/main`;
- canonical URL plus a pre-seeded remote-tracking ref;
- injected/global Git configuration that rewrites the canonical URL;
- existing empty directories;
- clone/update/global-link failures and managed retry replacement.

Interrupted state transitions are covered explicitly:

- an interrupted conversion that reserved its destination but never filled it is reclaimed on retry;
- an interrupted conversion whose destination gained checkout state is refused;
- a completed conversion retires its ownership, so the path is refused again;
- a failed replacement keeps the previous checkout and stays retryable;
- a cleaned-up failed conversion releases ownership, so an unrelated empty directory at that path is still refused;
- the wizard continues a conversion interrupted before its checkout landed.

The command-level suite also verifies refusal occurs before service mutation, follow-up fetches receive the sanitized Git environment, failed initial conversions clean up safely, service-repair-aware failures retain a usable target, and successful conversion retires retry ownership.

## Evidence

Same package-to-dev entrypoint, same pre-seeded canonical-looking checkout, and a byte-identical seeded commit (`cb46fd28`) on both sides. Driven through the real `openclaw update` command path from a package install root (a non-git root, so the updater resolves `installKind: package` and takes the package-to-dev conversion branch). Private paths are replaced with placeholders.

Hostile fixture in both runs: canonical `remote.origin.url`, `remote.origin.skipFetchAll=true`, a pre-seeded `refs/remotes/origin/main`, and a `PAYLOAD.txt` the canonical repository does not contain.

```text
BEFORE (pristine base 7cde0ac8c0) - the existing checkout is adopted
$ git -C $OPENCLAW_GIT_DIR config remote.origin.url
https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw.git
$ git -C $OPENCLAW_GIT_DIR config remote.origin.skipFetchAll
true
$ git -C $OPENCLAW_GIT_DIR rev-parse refs/remotes/origin/main
cb46fd28114f2f92783c352b390506b416720e7f
$ openclaw update --channel dev --yes
Updating OpenClaw...

Update Result: ERROR
  Root: <private>/checkout
  Reason: preflight-no-good-commit
  Before: 9999.0.0

Steps:
  OK   clean check (12ms)
  OK   git fetch (15ms)
  FAIL git show-ref main (10ms)
      fatal: 'refs/heads/main' - not a valid ref
  OK   git remote (9ms)
  FAIL upstream check (10ms)
      fatal: no such branch: 'main'
  OK   git rev-parse refs/remotes/origin/main (10ms)
  OK   git rev-list (11ms)
  OK   preflight worktree (20ms)
  OK   preflight checkout (cb46fd28) (12ms)
  OK   preflight deps install (cb46fd28) (402ms)
  FAIL preflight build (cb46fd28) (403ms)
  OK   preflight cleanup (11ms)

Total time: 1.82s
```

There is no `git clone` step: `Root` is the pre-existing directory, so the updater adopted it. `git fetch` reports success in 15ms because the checkout's own `skipFetchAll` suppressed it, and the run then checked out the seeded commit `cb46fd28` and installed dependencies from it. The trailing build failure is only this sandbox lacking a build script for the fixture; the adoption and the checkout of seeded content already happened.

```text
AFTER (this patch, head d6d958118d, identical inputs) - refused before any mutation
$ openclaw update --channel dev --yes
Updating OpenClaw...

Error: OPENCLAW_GIT_DIR already exists: <private>/checkout. Package-to-dev conversion
creates a fresh OpenClaw checkout and will not reuse existing directories. Move it or
set OPENCLAW_GIT_DIR to an unused path.
    at reserveGitCheckoutDir (<private>/openclaw/src/cli/update-cli/shared.ts:249:13)
    at async createGitCheckout (<private>/openclaw/src/cli/update-cli/shared.ts:295:5)
  [cause]: Error: EEXIST: file already exists, mkdir '<private>/checkout'
      at async reserveGitCheckoutDir (<private>/openclaw/src/cli/update-cli/shared.ts:243:5)
      at async createGitCheckout (<private>/openclaw/src/cli/update-cli/shared.ts:295:5)
      at async runGitUpdate (<private>/openclaw/src/cli/update-cli/update-command.ts:456:7)
      at async updateCommandInternal (<private>/openclaw/src/cli/update-cli/update-command.ts:1211:11)
      at async updateCommand (<private>/openclaw/src/cli/update-cli/update-command.ts:583:10)
    errno: -17, code: 'EEXIST', syscall: 'mkdir', path: '<private>/checkout'

$ git -C $OPENCLAW_GIT_DIR log --oneline -1
cb46fd2 seed hostile checkout
$ ls $OPENCLAW_GIT_DIR
PAYLOAD.txt package.json
```

The refusal comes from the reservation `mkdir` inside `createGitCheckout`, before any step runs against the directory, and the pre-existing checkout is left exactly as it was.

Same head, unused `OPENCLAW_GIT_DIR`, showing the reordered crash-safe conversion:

```text
AFTER (this patch, head d6d958118d) - fresh path clones for real
$ openclaw update --channel dev --yes
Updating OpenClaw...

Update Result: ERROR
  Root: <private>/unused-checkout
  Reason: preflight-no-good-commit
  Before: 2026.7.2

Steps:
  OK   git clone (174s)
  OK   clean check (1.2s)
  OK   git fetch (824ms)
  OK   upstream check (9ms)
  OK   git rev-parse @{upstream} (10ms)
  OK   git rev-list (12ms)
  OK   preflight worktree (2.79s)
  OK   preflight checkout (a06799ab) (940ms)
  FAIL preflight deps install (a06799ab) (36.36s)
  [9 further preflight checkout / deps install pairs elided; each install failed identically]
  OK   preflight cleanup (3.19s)

Total time: 324.47s
```

Observed while that clone was still running: the destination is reserved but still empty, the clone is staged out of place, and ownership is already recorded in the shared state database.

```text
$ ls -a <private>/fresh-parent
.
..
.unused-checkout.staging-dd7685e9-133e-45fe-893a-95d689fc5329
unused-checkout
$ du -sh <private>/fresh-parent/unused-checkout <private>/fresh-parent/.unused-checkout.staging-*
4.0K	<private>/fresh-parent/unused-checkout
124K	<private>/fresh-parent/.unused-checkout.staging-dd7685e9-133e-45fe-893a-95d689fc5329
$ node -e "... select plugin_id,namespace,value_json from plugin_state_entries where plugin_id='core:update-cli' ..."
[{"plugin_id":"core:update-cli","namespace":"managed-checkouts","value_json":"{\"token\":\"3af8bfdc-0b8e-48ed-bfbb-fd851284582e\",\"dir\":\"<private>/unused-checkout\",\"createdAtMs\":1784258040670}"}]
```

After the staging clone was swapped into place:

```text
$ ls -a <private>/fresh-parent
.
..
unused-checkout
$ ls -l <private>/unused-checkout/.git/.openclaw-update-managed
-rw------- 1 root root 37 Jul 17 03:16 <private>/unused-checkout/.git/.openclaw-update-managed
$ cat <private>/unused-checkout/.git/.openclaw-update-managed
3af8bfdc-0b8e-48ed-bfbb-fd851284582e
$ git -C <private>/unused-checkout config remote.origin.url
https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw.git
$ git -C <private>/unused-checkout config remote.origin.skipFetchAll; echo "(exit=$?)"
(exit=1)
```

The clone runs into `.unused-checkout.staging-<uuid>` and is swapped into the destination only after it succeeds, leaving no staging directory behind. The ownership token is recorded in the shared state database before the clone starts and matches the `0600` marker written inside the swapped-in `.git`. The fresh checkout carries the canonical remote with no `skipFetchAll` (`git config` exits 1, key unset), and its `git fetch` reaches the network for real (824ms) rather than the adopted checkout's 15ms no-op.

That conversion still ends in `ERROR` because dependency installation cannot run in this sandbox. The failure exercised the recovery path: the updater removed the checkout it had created and retired its ownership record, leaving nothing adopted.

```text

.
..
$ node -e "... select plugin_id,namespace,value_json from plugin_state_entries where plugin_id='core:update-cli' ..."

```

Not exercised: no successful end-to-end conversion, because dependency installation and the build/global-link steps cannot run in this sandbox; the `global install` step and ownership retirement on the success path were therefore not driven, and no managed-retry replacement of a previously owned checkout was driven through the command entrypoint.

## Validation

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/cli/update-cli/shared.git-checkout.test.ts`: 14 passed.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/cli/update-cli.test.ts`: 188 passed.
- `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.core.json`: exit 0.
- `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.core.test.json`: exit 0.
- `oxlint src/cli/update-cli/ src/infra/errors.ts` and `oxfmt --check`: clean.
- `node --import tsx scripts/check-import-cycles.ts`: 0 runtime value cycles.
- `node scripts/check-database-first-legacy-stores.mjs`: passed.

target.title: fix(codex): preserve paragraph boundaries in Codex runtime reply delivery (#109032)
target.body:
Closes #109032

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where WhatsApp installations using automatic visible replies with the Codex agent runtime would have multiple reply paragraphs collapsed into a single WhatsApp bubble, losing the intended conversational structure. The same configuration with the OpenClaw agent runtime correctly preserves separate bubbles.

The user-facing symptom is that the LLM's response structure (e.g., a bullet list or two distinct paragraphs) is lost when using the Codex runtime, even with `chunkMode: "newline"` and permissive block coalescing configured. The configured coalescing controls cannot recover paragraph boundaries after an earlier merge in the pipeline.

## Why This Change Was Made

Codex app-server produces a single `message_start`/`message_end` cycle per turn, accumulating all paragraphs into one assistant text entry with a shared `assistantMessageIndex`. The reply pipeline's cross-index flush mechanism (`block-reply-pipeline.ts:270-276`) relies on index changes to separate logical blocks, so Codex's single index causes all paragraphs to flow into the coalescer as one payload. OpenClaw runtime avoids this by producing multiple message cycles with distinct indexes.

The fix has two parts, both using the `\n\s*\n+` blank-line pattern that the codebase already uses in `EmbeddedBlockChunker` and Telegram rich blocks for the same purpose:

1. **Codex projection boundary** (`event-projector-assistant.ts`): `collectAssistantTexts()` now splits accumulated final text at paragraph boundaries, producing multiple `assistantTexts` entries instead of one. This matches the multi-entry surface that OpenClaw runtime produces.

2. **Shared payload builder** (`payloads.ts`): the `shouldUseCanonicalFinalAnswer` path (which uses `lastAssistant`'s full text when available) now also splits at paragraph boundaries. This prevents the canonical answer path from re-merging paragraphs that the projection layer correctly separated.

Neither change introduces Codex-specific logic to channel plugins or WhatsApp code. Both are bounded, narrow modifications that follow the same literal pattern as commit `8d46971129` (sanitize streamed text in the same pipeline) and commit `bafdec9868` (Codex + shared pipeline paired change).

## User Impact

WhatsApp users with Codex runtime and automatic visible replies will see reply paragraphs delivered as separate bubbles, matching the behavior they already get with the OpenClaw runtime. No configuration changes are needed. Non-Codex runtimes, single-paragraph replies, and media replies are unaffected.

## Evidence

**Real-behavior proof** — a standalone harness imports `buildEmbeddedRunPayloads` from production source (no mocks, no loaders) and verifies 10 scenarios / 24 assertions:

```
Self-check: loaded modified buildEmbeddedRunPayloads from file:///.../src/.../payloads.ts
[Scenario 1] Codex multi-paragraph + lastAssistant (canonical answer):  2 payloads
[Scenario 2] Multi-paragraph, no lastAssistant:                         2 payloads
[Scenario 3] Single paragraph (regression):                             1 payload
[Scenario 4] Three paragraphs:                                          3 payloads
[Scenario 5] Error state (not affected):                                payloads with isError
[Scenario 6] Multi-line without blank-line separator (regression):      1 payload (no split)
[Scenario 7] Blank line with whitespace as paragraph break:             2 payloads
[Scenario 8-10] Edge cases (empty, whitespace-only):                    correct filtering
=== 24 scenarios: 24 passed, 0 failed ===
```

**A/B proof** — same harness against `main` (without the fix) shows scenario 1/4/7 fail:
```
[Scenario 1] Expected 2 payloads, got 1  (text: "Paragraph 1\n\nParagraph 2")
[Scenario 4] Expected 3 payloads, got 1  (text: "A\n\nB\n\nC")
=== 24 scenarios: 14 passed, 10 failed ===
```

**Unit tests** — all pass:
- `payloads.test.ts` 54/54 ✅
- `payloads.errors.test.ts` 70/70 ✅
- `event-projector.test.ts` 164/164 ✅
- `block-reply-pipeline.test.ts` 21/21 ✅
- `chunk.test.ts` 68/68 ✅

**Scope guard** — `git diff --check` clean. No channel plugin, no config changes, no new configuration options. The only test update is one assertion in `event-projector.test.ts` that reflects the new multi-entry output for a multi-paragraph final answer.

---

This PR is AI-assisted. Analysis, implementation, and testing were performed using AI tools (opencode) with review by the author.

target.title: fix(doctor): preserve unparseable config instead of silently discarding it
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw doctor --fix` could silently destroy user config. In a home whose gateway had never started (no last-known-good promotion record), running `doctor --fix` on an unparseable `openclaw.json` declined recovery and wrote a stripped best-effort config — silently dropping the user's `gateway` and `models` sections — then exited 0, implying success.

## Why This Change Was Made

`recoverConfigFromLastKnownGood` returns false with no promotion record (promotion only happens on gateway startup), so doctor fell through to writing a gutted config without preserving the original. The promoted-recovery path already preserves the corrupt file as `.clobbered.*`; the never-promoted path did not. Now, when the config is unparseable and unrecoverable, doctor preserves the original as `.clobbered.*` and refuses to apply repairs, exiting non-zero with the preserved path — never silently discarding user sections. Extracts a shared `preserveConfigSnapshotAsClobbered` helper; the working promoted-recovery path is unchanged.

## User Impact

A corrupt config on a fresh/never-started install is preserved and surfaced loudly instead of being silently gutted. No change to the already-correct recovery path when the gateway has run before.

## Evidence

- Regression test `doctor-config-preflight.test.ts`: never-promoted + unparseable + `--fix` → original preserved as `.clobbered.*` (identical SHA-256) and non-zero exit; the silent-strip behavior no longer occurs. 38+7 tests pass.
- Real CLI black-box: exit 1, warning contains the exact `.clobbered.*` path, current+preserved files byte-identical.
- `node scripts/check-changed.mjs` green on Testbox; autoreview clean.

target.title: fix(security): scan SKILL.md text in skill code-safety audit
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw security audit --deep` never scanned a skill's SKILL.md. A malicious workspace SKILL.md containing pipe-to-shell install patterns (`curl … | bash`), `rm -rf ~/`, secret-exfiltration, or prompt-injection produced **zero** audit findings — while the identical patterns placed in a sibling `tool.js` were immediately flagged `skills.code_safety critical`. Since SKILL.md is the primary (often only) file a skill ships, and manually-authored workspace skills are never scanned at install time, malicious skill text was invisible to the audit.

## Why This Change Was Made

The scanner already has rules written for skill *text* (`shell-pipe-to-shell` = "Skill text includes pipe-to-shell install pattern", `secret-exfiltration`, `prompt-injection-*`), and the Workshop proposal path scans PROPOSAL.md markdown. But the installed/workspace-skill audit (`collectInstalledSkillsCodeSafetyFindings`) only fed `SCANNABLE_EXTENSIONS` (JS/TS) to the scanner, skipping the markdown.

Fix: each audited skill's SKILL.md content is now scanned through `scanSkillContent` + `scanSource` (the same scanners the Workshop uses), merged into the code-safety summary. Scoped to the skills audit path — the global directory scanner's extension set is unchanged, so READMEs/docs elsewhere are not newly scanned (no false-positive flood).

## User Impact

`security audit --deep` now flags dangerous instructions in skill SKILL.md files (pipe-to-shell, prompt-injection, exfiltration), closing a security blind spot for manually-authored/workspace skills. No change to non-skill scanning.

## Evidence

- Regression test `audit-extra.async.test.ts` "scans SKILL.md text for dangerous skill instructions": **red before** ("expected skill markdown code-safety finding"), green after. 7 tests pass.
- `node scripts/check-changed.mjs` green on Testbox; `oxfmt --check`, `git diff --check` clean.

target.title: fix(reef): add timeout and bounded JSON reads to relay transport
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The Reef relay transport client (`extensions/reef/src/transport.ts`) calls `fetch` with no timeout. A relay that black-holes the TCP/TLS handshake or stalls before returning headers will hang `ReefInboxConnection.drain()` forever, silently killing the reconnect/backoff loop.

## Why This Change Was Made

This follows the same pattern as recent merged fixes that bound network operations (e.g., #106035, #105885, #102865). The change wraps relay requests in `fetchWithTimeout` (15 s) using the existing injectable `fetcher`, so tests can stub stalled responses. Bounded JSON response reads already landed on `main` via #106456 (16 MiB success / 64 KiB error caps through `readProviderJsonResponse`); this PR adds only the missing request timeout on top of them.

## User Impact

- Prevents silent channel death when the Reef relay becomes unresponsive.
- No behavior change for healthy relays; a stall surfaces as a `TimeoutError` at the 15 s deadline and triggers the existing reconnect path.

## Evidence

- New test covers a stalled relay timing out after 15 s; existing main-side tests cover the bounded JSON reads.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/reef/src/transport.test.ts --run` — 10/10 tests passed on the exact head.

target.title: fix(codex): bound app-server websocket handshake waits to requestTimeoutMs
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators using Codex app-server over websocket/unix transport would hang forever on initialize/RPC when a peer accepted the socket but never completed the WebSocket upgrade.

## Why This Change Was Made

Bound upgrades with `ws.handshakeTimeout` **and** an explicit CONNECTING deadline at the transport chokepoint (`createWebSocketTransport`). `ws.handshakeTimeout` alone does **not** abort custom `createConnection` (Unix) upgrades - verified with a never-upgrade peer that stayed CONNECTING past the library timeout.

Production budget is resolved `appServer.requestTimeoutMs` (default 60s) from `CodexAppServerClient.start` via `resolveCodexAppServerRuntimeOptions()`.

**Narrowed to Codex-only (Maintainer option 1, recommended):** Removed the unrelated APNs CodeQL allowlist (`#109357`) and docs-sync typings export (`#109364`) that prior heads bundled to unblock CI. Those are main pre-existing debt and should land independently. This branch now touches only Codex runtime, Codex tests, and the Codex harness doc.

Documented the expanded `requestTimeoutMs` contract in `docs/plugins/codex-harness.md` so operators know it also bounds WebSocket/Unix upgrade handshakes.

Collision check: [#108795](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/108795) closed unmerged; APNs allowlist split [#109357](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/109357); typings unblocker [#109364](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/109364).

## User Impact

- **Before:** never-upgrade peers hang initialize/RPC forever (TCP and Unix).
- **After:** handshake follows operator `requestTimeoutMs` (default 60s) on both TCP and Unix, then emits transport exit (`1006`).

## Verification

## Real behavior proof

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where GitHub Copilot usage checks could leave the HTTP response body open when the usage endpoint returned a non-success status. Repeated failed checks could retain connections until the request timeout elapsed.

## Why This Change Was Made

The failed-response path now cancels the unused body before returning the existing HTTP error snapshot; successful response parsing is unchanged. The main risk is changing error reporting while releasing the stream, so the regression test and loopback proof verify that `HTTP 500` is preserved while the connection closes.

## User Impact

Failed GitHub Copilot usage checks release their network connection promptly instead of holding it open until timeout, while returning the same error result to users.

## Evidence

On Linux with Node 24.18.0, I drove the real exported `fetchCopilotUsage` against a real `node:http` loopback server that returned HTTP 500 and kept writing its body. The only injected seam redirected the function's fetch URL to that loopback server; the request, response stream, and TCP socket were real.

Before, on current `upstream/main` (`730cfd774d6`), the function returned the expected error but the server still had one active socket after 300 ms:

```text
{"revision":"upstream/main@730cfd774d6","status":"HTTP 500","returnMs":24,"responseClosedWithin300Ms":false,"activeSocketsAfter300Ms":1}
```

After, on patched HEAD (`1d27f84fd2d3`), the same harness preserved the error and observed the response close within 300 ms with no active sockets:

```text
{"revision":"patched HEAD","status":"HTTP 500","returnMs":27,"responseClosedWithin300Ms":true,"activeSocketsAfter300Ms":0}
```

Focused regression test:

```text
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/github-copilot/models.test.ts
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests  33 passed (33)
```

Changed-surface checks passed, including extension production/test typechecks, formatting, lint, plugin boundaries, and import-cycle checks:

```text
OPENCLAW_CHECK_CHANGED_REMOTE_CHILD=1 pnpm check:changed --base upstream/main -- extensions/github-copilot/usage.ts extensions/github-copilot/models.test.ts
```

Live GitHub Copilot credentials were not used; the changed branch runs only after an HTTP response is received, and the loopback proof exercises that response-body lifecycle directly.

AI-assisted: Codex helped inspect and implement the change; the loopback proof and validation commands above were run manually.

target.title: fix(pr-gates): accept a green ci-gate check without waiting for the full CI run
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`scripts/pr prepare-run` requires the `CI` **workflow-run object** to be `completed`. That object stays open while any job in the run executes — including post-gate stragglers — and flips back to `in_progress` when a single flaky job is rerun, even though `openclaw/ci-gate` (the merge button's signal) already succeeded for the head. Result: agent landings block on a green button until the last slow non-gating lane drains (maintainer-reported today; it has repeatedly stretched landing latency into merge-drift territory).

## Why This Change Was Made

The hosted gate verifier gains a second, tightly-scoped CI acceptance path. When the recent CI run for the head is not completed-successful, it consults the head's check runs (`filter=latest`, paginated by `total_count`) and accepts iff the **`openclaw/ci-gate` check** — which `needs` every merge-blocking job, so its success IS the green button — is completed, successful, and within the existing 24-hour freshness window (`completed_at`, same clock-skew rule).

Hardening from three adversarial review rounds, all fixed with regression tests:

- **No spoofing**: the check must come from the selected CI run's own `check_suite_id` AND the `github-actions` app — a foreign app or workflow publishing a check named `openclaw/ci-gate` reads as `missing`.
- **Fail closed**: check-runs fetch errors or malformed pages throw; they never grant passage.
- **Terminal non-success blocks hard**: a `failure`, `timed_out`, `cancelled`, or any other completed non-success gate on the current head throws immediately, so the previous-head (docs-only) evidence fallback can never mask a red gate.
- **Advisory reds don't block**: failed checks from other workflows/apps (periphery scans etc.) neither grant nor block this path — exactly matching the button semantics that motivated the fix.

The completed-run fast path is byte-for-byte unchanged and performs no additional API calls; evidence JSON records which path passed (`ciEvidence: "workflow-run" | "ci-gate-check"` + the gate's `completed_at`).

## User Impact

Maintainer/agent landings via `scripts/pr` proceed as soon as the merge button is green and fresh (≤24h) instead of idling behind non-gating stragglers or run-level rerun churn. No behavior change for red, stale, or still-pending gates; scheduled Testbox gate rules are untouched.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/verify-pr-hosted-gates.test.ts` — 54/54 pass (new: in-progress-run + green gate acceptance, advisory-red tolerance, spoofed app/suite rejection, failed/timed-out/cancelled gate blocking incl. the previous-head-fallback bypass regression, staleness at the 24h boundary, fast-path fetcher-not-called, fetch-error fail-closed).
- `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs scripts/verify-pr-hosted-gates.mjs` clean; oxfmt clean; `git diff --check` clean.
- Autoreview (Codex, gpt-5.6-sol, xhigh): four rounds — surfaced the advisory-red over-blocking, the check-name spoofing hole, and the cancelled-conclusion fallback bypass; all fixed with tests; final pass clean (0.87).
- GitHub REST semantics (filter=latest, 100-item pages, workflow-run `check_suite_id`, check-run `check_suite`/`app`) verified against current docs during review.

target.title: fix(transport): preserve HTTP status and Retry-After on Anthropic errors
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #103849

On the default Anthropic Messages transport, a 429 response with a `Retry-After` header is turned into a plain `Error` with no status code or retry-after info. `AgentSession.prepareRetry` then falls back to fixed 2s/4s/8s exponential backoff regardless of the server's cooldown, causing all 3 retries to land inside the still-active rate-limit window.

## Fix

1. **Preserve**: parse `Retry-After` (delta-seconds or HTTP-date) and attach `status` + `retryAfterMs` to the thrown error in `createAnthropicMessagesClient`.
2. **Thread**: extract `retryAfterMs` onto the transport output and add optional field to `AssistantMessage`.
3. **Consume**: `prepareRetry` now uses `message.retryAfterMs` (clamped to 60s) via extracted `resolveAutoRetryDelayMs` helper, falling back to exponential backoff when absent.

## Evidence

**Unit tests** (`anthropic-transport-stream.test.ts` + `sdk.test.ts`):
- 136 total passed
- 3 new stub-server 429 tests: delta-seconds `Retry-After: 30`, HTTP-date format, no `Retry-After` header
- `prepareRetry` tests proving `delayMs === retryAfterMs` (30s honored) and clamp/fallback behavior

**Quality gates**:
- `oxlint` — exit 0
- `oxfmt --check` — exit 0  
- `tsgo:core` + `check:test-types` — exit 0

**Changed files**: 6 (`packages/llm-core/src/types.ts`, `src/agents/transport-stream-shared.ts`, `src/agents/anthropic-transport-stream.ts`, `src/agents/sessions/agent-session-execution.ts`, + 2 test files)

target.title: fix(imessage): bound drop diagnostic dedupe
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

- **Fixes an issue where users running a long-lived iMessage monitor could retain one throttled diagnostic key for every conversation ever seen.**
- **Affected surface / workflow:** inbound iMessage notifications dropped as `from me` and logged once per conversation.
- **Root cause, in product terms:** `loggedThrottledDropDiagnostics` was a monitor-lifetime `Set` keyed by account, conversation, and reason, with no eviction.
- **Why it matters / User impact:** gateways that encounter many distinct chats can accumulate process-lifetime diagnostic state even though only recent warn-once suppression is operationally useful.

## Why This Change Was Made

- **Fix classification:** Root cause fix
- **Complete shipped solution:** replace the unbounded `Set` with the existing bounded dedupe cache, capped at 512 entries with no TTL.
- **Why this is root-cause fix:** retention is bounded at the state owner while the existing warn-once behavior remains unchanged for recent conversations.
- **Key design boundary / source of truth:** the cap matches the existing iMessage per-chat allowlist warning cache; eviction only allows an old conversation to emit one diagnostic again.
- **Non-goals / what did not change:** drop classification, loop rate limiting, diagnostic content, and non-throttled diagnostics are unchanged.
- **Compatibility, merge-risk, or maintainer-decision notes:** no public API or configuration changes; the behavioral difference is limited to re-logging an evicted old conversation.

## User Impact

- **Users/operators/developers can now:** keep long-lived iMessage monitors bounded when many distinct conversations produce throttled drop diagnostics.
- **Existing behavior preserved:** duplicate `from me` diagnostics remain suppressed for recently active conversations.
- **What was not tested or remains unavailable:** no real Messages database or signed-in macOS Messages session was used; the live proof used a local JSON-RPC `imsg` fixture process through the production RPC client and monitor path.

## Evidence

- **Environment:** Windows Git Bash, Node.js 24.18.0; history-preserving merge with `origin/main` `e6f4e27c6ea285d209f64443eb247994ad973972`; local JSON-RPC child process implementing the `imsg rpc --json` boundary.
- **Commands run after this patch:** `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/imessage/src/monitor.watch-subscribe-retry.test.ts`; `pnpm format:check`; prior `node --import tsx` live monitor proof using the production `IMessageRpcClient`. `pnpm check:changed -- ...` was attempted but its delegated Blacksmith Testbox helper was unavailable locally, so it is disclosed rather than reported as passing.
- **Key results / observations:** the current-main focused suite passed `4/4`; the overflow regression processed 513 distinct `from me` conversations, re-logged the oldest after eviction, retained recent suppression, and directly awaited each monitor callback before asserting the final duplicate. The prior production-path fixture reported no runtime errors (`diagnostics=514`, `distinctChatIds=513`).
- **Review findings addressed, if any:** resolved the current-main test conflict without dropping its redaction coverage, made the monitor callback awaitable without changing client concurrency semantics, directly awaited the final suppressed notification, and retained the bounded 512-entry cache behavior. A final open-PR search found no exact overlap for `loggedThrottledDropDiagnostics`.
- **Regression guardrail:** the monitor-path test overflows the 512-entry cache and verifies both oldest-entry eviction and recent-entry suppression.
- **Patch quality notes:** two focused files; no dependency, schema, configuration, or lockfile changes.
- **Latest-main conflict resolution:** current main added a production-path redaction regression and the `expectDefined` helper import. The resolved branch keeps both, adds bounded-cache overflow/recency coverage, and preserves the hosted PR ancestry through a merge commit.
- **Maintainer-ready confidence:** code and focused proof are high confidence; a real signed-in macOS Messages monitor remains unavailable in this Windows environment and is explicitly left as a maintainer/external proof gate.

target.title: fix(config): restore env changes before rethrowing INVALID_CONFIG
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`loadConfigFromContext()` (previously `loadConfigLocal()`) applies `env.vars` to `process.env`
during config resolution via `resolveConfigForRead()` → `applyConfigEnvVars()`. The catch
block only restored env changes for `INVALID_CONFIG`, leaving other post-resolution failures
(`DuplicateAgentDirError`, unexpected exceptions) to leak env side effects into the running
process.

**Trigger**: `openclaw.json` with valid `env.vars` entries but other config errors
(e.g. invalid `gateway.port`, duplicate `agentDir` values).

## Why This Change Was Made

Other code paths in the config loader already follow the correct pattern of calling
`restoreEnvChangesIfUnchanged()` before returning/retrying after config operations that
modify env (suspicious recovery retry, write rollback). The original fix only covered
`INVALID_CONFIG`. The shared catch path now restores env for every failed config load,
with a null guard so `maybeLoadDotEnvForConfig()` failures (which happen before any
config env mutations are applied) are unaffected.

The fix follows the same pattern in the refactored code at `src/config/io.load.ts`
(function was previously `loadConfigLocal()` in `src/config/io.ts`). `envBeforeRead`
is hoisted to function scope so the `catch` block can access it.

## User Impact

- Before: any non-INVALID_CONFIG failure with `env.vars` → env leaked → subsequent
  operations see wrong env values
- After: env is properly restored before any rethrow, matching the behavior of all
  other error/retry paths

## Evidence

### Focused Regression Tests

`src/config/io.invalid-config-env-restore.test.ts` — 6 tests, all passing:

1. `restoreEnvChangesIfUnchanged` unit: removes newly injected key
2. `restoreEnvChangesIfUnchanged` unit: restores overwritten key
3. `restoreEnvChangesIfUnchanged` unit: preserves externally modified key (TOCTOU-safe)
4. Integration: valid `env.vars` + invalid `gateway.port` → env restored on INVALID_CONFIG
5. Integration: env key with pre-existing value overwritten by config → restored on INVALID_CONFIG
6. Integration: valid `env.vars` + duplicate `agentDir` → env restored on DuplicateAgentDirError

```
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/config/io.invalid-config-env-restore.test.ts
Test Files  1 passed (1)
     Tests  6 passed (6)
```

### Lint & Format

```
oxlint --tsconfig config/tsconfig/oxlint.core.json src/config/io.load.ts src/config/io.invalid-config-env-restore.test.ts  # passes clean
oxfmt --check src/config/io.load.ts src/config/io.invalid-config-env-restore.test.ts                                      # passes clean
```

### Rebase

Rebased onto latest `upstream/main` (0a19e1ed586) to resolve merge conflict.
The fix was adapted to the refactored config loader structure where `loadConfigLocal()`
moved from `src/config/io.ts` into `loadConfigFromContext()` in `src/config/io.load.ts`.

## Files Changed

| File | +/- | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `src/config/io.load.ts` | +14 -1 | Hoist envBeforeRead to function scope; restore env in shared catch |
| `src/config/io.invalid-config-env-restore.test.ts` | +129 | Unit + integration tests for env restore on all config load failures |

target.title: feat(channels): core-owned durable ingress drain — one turn-adoption lifecycle, Telegram first
target.body:
Closes #108656

AI-assisted: yes. Implemented by grok-4.5 under Claude orchestration; every phase was structurally reviewed, adversarially re-reviewed per commit (Codex `gpt-5.6-sol` high), and independently validated before inclusion.

> **Scope note:** per ClawSweeper's review recommendation (option 3) and maintainer decision, the WhatsApp migration was split out of this PR. Core + Telegram land here; WhatsApp follows in its own PR once the QA-lab live WhatsApp lane is re-linked (the shared broker's Baileys sessions are logged out). The split-out work — including fixes for two real WhatsApp adapter bugs found during validation (accept-path drain-idle await blocking multi-message upserts; dispatch-side re-normalization dropping messages whose LID mapping resolved only at receive time) — is preserved on branch `wa-durable-drain-followup` with the full WhatsApp suite green.

## What Problem This Solves

Telegram was the only channel with a private transport-level turn-lifecycle layer (reply fence, ingress spool, per-transport claim/replay/watchdog loops duplicated across polling and webhook). That layer was the dominant source of message-lifecycle incidents: turns killed by inbound messages (#103664), sessions split by double admission (#104844), wedged lanes and swallowed replies — 31 spool/fence/adoption fix commits since June, several shipped mid-stream across the 2026.7.1 betas, with user reports still arriving on 2026.7.1. Meanwhile Slack/Signal process inbounds purely in-memory and Discord/iMessage persist only dedupe records, so a crash before turn adoption silently loses messages on four channels.

## Why This Change Was Made

The reliability concepts were channel-agnostic but the implementation was Telegram-private and written twice. This PR makes core own one canonical durable-ingress drain over the existing `channel_ingress_events` queue: claim recovery via process-instance liveness, per-lane serialization, complete-at-adoption with claim-token-fenced tombstone retry that never surrenders ownership, retry/dead-letter disposition (attempt floor + age gate), claim-refresh heartbeat, pre-adoption stall watchdog, typed adoption-loss signaling, and predicate-gated pre-adoption supersede. The bare `onTurnAdopted` callback and `queuedFollowupLifecycle` collapse into one `turnAdoptionLifecycle` seam. Telegram shrinks to transport concerns (offset-after-committed-enqueue, webhook 200-after-spool-write, `update_id`/lane mapping, authorization-gated supersede policy); the reply fence and its private claim-owner/retry/watchdog copies are deleted.

The reliability invariants from `extensions/telegram/AGENTS.md` are now core contract tests (`src/channels/message/ingress-drain.test.ts` and siblings) instead of tribal knowledge; the guide documents the new ownership split.

## User Impact

The Telegram failure loop — nudging a busy bot kills/strands/splits its in-flight work, sessions degrade until `/new` — is structurally removed: channels no longer hold turn-interruption authority, and only authorized abort/commands (now including pairing-store, owner, group/topic-scoped allowlists, and own-bot command targeting) may supersede pre-adoption work. Message durability semantics (at-least-once, no replay of adopted turns, no silent loss on transient failures) are enforced in one place, and the other channels — WhatsApp first (follow-up branch ready), then Discord/Slack/Signal/iMessage — can adopt the same seam with a small adapter.

LOC: total net −470 (+5,125/−5,595); Telegram prod −1,012, core drain +952 shared by six channels.

## Evidence

- Blacksmith Testbox full gate on the final stack: pairing-store auth guard, `pnpm tsgo` prod + test lanes, `pnpm plugin-sdk:surface:check`, `pnpm build`, and `pnpm test src/channels extensions/telegram extensions/whatsapp extensions/voice-call src/auto-reply src/gateway src/plugins src/plugin-sdk` — all green except two failures proven pre-existing on clean `origin/main` (`commands-plugins.install.test.ts` from #102197; `npm-install-security-scan.release.test.ts` google-meet dangerous-exec hit from #109413/#109466 — this diff touches neither).
- Core drain contract tests: crash-window replay-exactly-once, complete-at-adoption, deferral holds claim, watchdog-through-deferral, supersede tombstones, dead-letter age gate, claim-token-fenced completion, two-drains-no-steal, heartbeat reclaim guillotine.
- Telegram transport proof: offset-after-spool-ack, webhook redelivery on write failure, `update_id`/lane mapping, authorization-gated supersede incl. paired-DM/owner/topic-override/other-bot cases.
- Structured per-commit review (Codex `gpt-5.6-sol`, high reasoning) across every phase; 29 accepted findings — including the four lifecycle races ClawSweeper confirmed — fixed with per-failure-window regression tests.
- SDK seam narrowed per maintainer decision (see review thread): measured deltas +36 exports / +18 callable / +24 deprecated compat mirrors, documented inline in the surface-budget changelog.
- Live behavior proof on real Telegram from this branch (see review thread): nudge-during-turn survives with both replies exactly-once (run M3TTZH), and a SIGKILL 400 ms after an inbound replays exactly-once after restart (run C9BTFU).
